scenes.title: Mobile Web Controller & Remote Peripheral Suite

subtitles.text: Hello everyone, and welcome to our demonstration of WHID-Guard: an ESP32-S3 Phone-Controlled USB HID Keyboard and Mouse platform with BadUSB Simulation and a Defensive Keystroke Firewall.
Developed by Ram Karthik G and Harini V from the Department of Cybersecurity at Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, Chennai.
Modern operating systems implicitly trust Human Interface Devices, allowing unauthorized hardware implants to inject destructive payloads at microsecond bus speeds without host consent.
WHID-Guard provides an interruptible hardware emulation suite paired with an intelligent, per-device behavioral defense.
The system is powered by the ESP32-S3 dual-core microcontroller running at 240 megahertz with native USB-OTG full-speed hardware directly on GPIO 19 and 20.
Our custom dual-port topology cleanly isolates attack vectors from developer controls.
The primary USB-OTG port connects to the target laptop, enumerating immediately as a standard driverless composite HID keyboard and multi-button mouse.

Concurrently, the CP210x UART bridge on Port 1 provides isolated serial telemetry and firmware flashing on COM5, ensuring continuous laboratory monitoring without disrupting the target host's USB bus.
Inside the firmware, an 8-state deterministic Finite State Machine governs scenario lifecycles.

Upon initial connection, it enforces a bounded 3.5-second wait for host USB enumeration to stabilize, and then automatically executes Scenario 1: an educational Notepad security awareness notification.
The platform includes four demonstration scenarios: Notepad awareness, institutional portal redirection, simulated PowerShell ransomware alerts, and Wi-Fi profile reconnaissance.
Scenarios can also be advanced offline using the physical GPIO 0 BOOT button, which employs a 50-millisecond hardware debounce filter.
Concurrently, the ESP32-S3 broadcasts a 2.4 gigahertz Wi-Fi network, hosting a responsive dark-mode Single-Page Application served entirely from PROGMEM flash memory.
Users authenticate against our REST API using a secure PIN, which issues tokenized credentials.

The interface features one-touch scenario execution with live status polling, a complete 6-row QWERTY keyboard with latched modifiers and system shortcuts, a 256-character bulk text transmitter, and a 60-hertz virtual trackpad mouse with relative motion clamping and precision drag-lock controls.
Standard BadUSB tools inject keystrokes at rigid 10-millisecond intervals, making them trivial to block with rudimentary speed limiters.
To rigorously test defensive resilience, we implemented an adversarial stealth mode in the ESP32-S3 firmware.

When toggled from the mobile interface, the controller replaces deterministic timing with stochastic jitter and automatically injects cognitive micro-pauses of 150 to 300 milliseconds following whitespace and punctuation marks, mimicking the natural neuromuscular delays of human operators.
To counter these sophisticated threats, we developed the WHID-Guard host defense engine.
Rather than relying on simplistic rate limits, WHID-Guard computes behavioral keystroke dynamics over an online sliding window of ten events.
It continuously calculates the mean Inter-Key Interval, standard deviation, coefficient of variation, and burst typing rate.

While human typing exhibits natural cognitive variance with a coefficient of variation exceeding 0.30, unconstrained BadUSB injection demonstrates rigid consistency below 0.15, enabling precise algorithmic classification without false alarms.
Traditional security tools install global keyboard hooks that lock out all typing indiscriminately.
WHID-Guard solves this problem through per-device hardware attribution via the Windows Raw Input API.
By registering for raw input message sinks and querying device names, our engine extracts the physical hardware device handle and USB Vendor and Product IDs.
When an injection attack is detected, our low-level keyboard hook drops only the malicious hardware packets, keeping the user's legitimate laptop keyboard completely active and responsive.
We conducted an extensive empirical evaluation across a 1,500-keystroke benchmark corpus.
On human baseline typing, WHID-Guard achieved a 0.0 percent False Positive Rate across 500 consecutive keystrokes.

Against unconstrained BadUSB attacks, the system achieved a 98.6 percent True Positive Detection Rate, quarantining the offending implant within exactly 8 characters—less than 85 milliseconds of total execution time.
Against stealth cadence emulation, it successfully flagged 25.2 percent of suspicious events.
In conclusion, WHID-Guard bridges offensive hardware exploration and host-level defensive resilience.
Our complete research manuscript and reproducible codebase are open-sourced on GitHub.
Thank you for your evaluation of our project.
